newsitem.title: KENYA: IMF decision to halt aid shakes Kenya.
newsitem.headline: IMF decision to halt aid shakes Kenya.

text.p: An IMF decision to halt a key aid package because of corruption shook Kenya on Friday, forcing the government to tighten belts to cover some of the loss put at $215 million this year.
Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said the government had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF halted its aid on Thursday.
"The government will concurrently cut its expenditure for this year and take revenue measures sufficient to address the shortfall of $141 million in external funding," he said in a statement.
Mudavadi said the government was committed to stability in the face of the IMF move and would open talks on an IMF "shadow" programme that would set targets for Kenya to meet for aid.

"The impact of the shortfall of $74 million which was expected from the IMF to support the balance of payments will have to be addressed by market forces in both the foreign exchange and domestic money markets without compromising the objective of maintaining price stability," he said.
Speaking before Mudavadi's steps, Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem called for urgent damage limitation and said the IMF dealt a serious blow to Kenya's international credibility.
"This is an unfortunate development but we must face it. We must not condemn (the IMF). What is important is damage limitation that will ensure the economy is not severely hurt," he told Reuters.

The IMF said on Thursday a $205 million three-year loan, offered under its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), was allowed to lapse because the response of President Daniel arap Moi's government to a deadline had been inadequate.
The Kenyan shilling opened at 59/59.50 to the dollar but weakened to 60/62.50 in 20 minutes. It later recovered to 61.50 -- 4.38 percent weaker than Thursday's close of 58.92.
But analysts estimated the IMF move would cost hundreds of millions of dollars in lost investment and foreign bilateral donors would also have a reason to cut aid to the country.
The IMF turned down a request from Moi's government for more time to try to take measures to meet IMF concerns about corruption and its demands for reform of the energy sector.
At the Nairobi Stock Exchange, brokers watched an empty board for deals by foreigners. "Foreign investors don't want to put their money into a sea of uncertainty," said one broker.

"Short term foreign investors will leave mainly because they are people who do not necessarily know the country too well and are coming in on the basis of an IMF programme," said a top market analyst, who declined to be named.
Kenya's opposition hailed the IMF decision, saying it would hit projects and investment but damage was necessary to pressure the government into reforms before a general election this year.

"I'm very pleased the IMF has finally recognised the enormous problem of governance in this country," said Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party which campaigned for political reforms and against corruption.
"We have been asking the IMF for a very long time to take this measure and obviously it will hit a lot of projects," he told Reuters. "Corruption was absolutely central to the IMF decision."
An opposition-backed alliance campaigning for political reforms has called for a nationwide general strike on August 8 to put more pressure on Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.

Foreign investors and tourists were already rattled by clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in June and July which culminated on July 7 with the deaths of at least nine people in Kenya's worst political unrest in seven years.
In an editorial written before news of the IMF decision, the independent Daily Nation newspaper said on Friday the IMF clearly believed the government was loathe to punish high-level corruption.
The IMF has focused on a scandal involving Goldenberg International to illustrate how authorities were wary about cracking down on corruption.
Goldenberg International was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under a compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and no diamonds.
The opposition had cited alleged links to powerful Kenyan politicians as the main reason why the Goldenberg case was not resolved.
